content: Following randomization, the rate of postnatal HIV transmission was found to be extremely low, with no significant difference observed between infants who received extended nevirapine (NVP) prophylaxis and those who received a placebo. In a large European cohort of high-risk mother-infant pairs, no differences in serious adverse events were noted among infants who received one, two, or three antiretroviral drugs. When comparing the occurrence of neutropenia between the two-drug and three-drug regimens, there was a trend toward more events in the three-drug group, but this difference was not statistically significant. A single-arm study conducted in Thailand on non-breastfeeding infants born to mothers who received less than eight weeks of antepartum antiretroviral therapy (ART) provided intensified infant prophylaxis with zidovudine (AZT), lamivudine (3TC), and NVP for two weeks, followed by AZT and 3TC for an additional two weeks. No intrapartum infections were observed, and the rate of serious adverse events in infants receiving this intensified prophylaxis was lower than in historical observational cohorts. None of the reviewed studies specifically addressed infants identified as HIV-exposed during the postpartum period or those exposed to an incident maternal HIV infection during pregnancy or breastfeeding. However, the findings from the systematic review may be applicable to these scenarios. Recommendations for extended prophylaxis in breastfeeding infants are based on the assumption that maternal ART is initiated at or before the start of infant prophylaxis, whether at birth or when maternal HIV is first detected postpartum. Infant prophylaxis is intended to provide temporary protection while maternal viral load decreases on ART. The 2016 WHO consolidated HIV guidelines highlight various factors to assess risk in HIV-exposed infants, including examples from countries that stratify infants by risk. Factors such as prolonged rupture of membranes, preterm delivery, and low birth weight are no longer associated with increased transmission risk when mothers are on ART. In the ART era, the primary determinants of transmission risk are maternal viral load and the duration of maternal ART. If viral load testing is unavailable, priority should be given to processing viral load specimens and results for pregnant and breastfeeding women. The 2021 WHO clinical guidelines recommend viral load testing for all pregnant women, regardless of ART initiation timing, at 34–36 weeks of gestation (or at delivery at the latest) to identify women at risk of treatment failure or those who may deliver infants at higher risk of perinatal transmission. High-risk infants are defined as those born to women with established HIV infection who received less than four weeks of ART before delivery, those with a maternal viral load >1,000 copies/mL within four weeks of delivery, those born to women with incident HIV infection during pregnancy or breastfeeding, or those born to women newly identified as HIV-positive postpartum. Administering multiple drugs to newborns poses operational challenges. While AZT and NVP are recommended based on available data, their differing dosing schedules (once daily for NVP and twice daily for AZT) complicate administration. Provider training and innovative dosing approaches, such as twice-daily NVP, may simplify implementation. When the recommended regimen is unavailable, alternative options like raltegravir (RAL), 3TC, lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r), or fixed-dose combinations containing AZT, NVP, and 3TC may be considered. Consistent with early infant diagnosis recommendations, no specific testing approach is advised for high-risk newborns, though birth diagnostic nucleic acid testing (NAT) may be considered. Infants identified as HIV-exposed postpartum have a high cumulative risk of already acquiring HIV by the time prophylaxis is initiated, and an HIV NAT test should be performed at the time of initiating prophylaxis. National programs could consider allowing clinical providers the option to extend infant prophylaxis beyond the recommended 6or 12-week period, with clearly defined scenarios warranting such continuation. Research gaps include the need for clinical and pharmacological studies to develop improved antiretroviral formulations for newborns and infants, including fixed-dose combinations. Studies on alternative drugs with better tolerability and efficacy for infant prophylaxis, such as integrase inhibitors, are also needed. Additionally, research is required to evaluate the clinical relevance of postnatal viremic episodes in breastfeeding mothers and their contribution to infant HIV infection, as well as the potential added benefit of enhanced prophylaxis in populations with effective maternal ART programs but known adherence challenges. Implementation science research should focus on defining high-risk infants in the context of universal maternal ART and evaluating service delivery models to improve adherence to enhanced postnatal prophylaxis and retention in care. Improving service delivery and implementing a comprehensive postnatal care package is essential to address barriers to effective infant HIV services. Socioeconomic and traditional factors that keep mother-infant pairs together can enhance service uptake. Programs should integrate effective interventions into service packages, combining facility-based and community-based approaches to support service provision and community engagement.g.g., point-of-care testing, provider training, enhanced counseling, and peer support). Community engagement and community-based services play a critical role in supporting HIV-exposed infant care. Networks of women living with HIV have been effective in improving community HIV literacy, forming support groups, strengthening care linkages, and reducing loss to follow-up among mother-infant pairs. Providing a comprehensive, integrated postnatal HIV service package can improve HIV outcomes and early childhood development overall.
